title: Tata Sons Posts ₹32,000 Crore Profit in FY26 as Air India Losses Balloon to Record Levels
excerpt: The Tata holding company's standalone profit surged 22% to ₹32,000 crore, but Air India's estimated ₹22,000 crore loss and a leadership vacuum at the airline cast a shadow over the recovery.
body:
• Tata Sons' standalone net profit rose roughly 22% to an estimated ₹32,000 crore in FY26, up from ₹26,232 crore in FY25, driven by strong performances across TCS, Tata Motors, Titan, and a successful Tata Capital listing.
  • Air India posted a record loss of approximately ₹22,000 crore ($2.4 billion) in the fiscal year ending March 2026 — far exceeding the airline's earlier internal estimate of $1.6 billion.
  • Tata Group and minority stakeholder Singapore Airlines (25.1% stake) are in discussions to inject fresh capital into Air India, according to Bloomberg.
  • The holding company more than doubled its dividend to Tata Trusts to over ₹3,000 crore, while total group dividend inflows reached ₹32,500 crore.

A Two-Speed Conglomerate

Tata Sons, the holding company of India's largest conglomerate, delivered a strong recovery in FY26, with standalone income from operations climbing to approximately ₹42,000 crore and net profit reaching an estimated ₹32,000 crore. The numbers mark a sharp rebound from FY25, when profit fell 24% to ₹26,232 crore and revenue dropped 12% to ₹38,835 crore.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=CgKlKN3aClI

The turnaround was powered by the group's listed heavyweights. Tata Consultancy Services, Tata Motors, Titan, Tata Power, Tata Steel, Tata Consumer, and Indian Hotels all delivered what executives described as "robust growth." Tata Capital's IPO, which raised nearly ₹7,500 crore, provided an additional one-time boost.

Tata Sons more than doubled its dividend payout to principal shareholder Tata Trusts, paying over ₹3,000 crore compared to ₹1,414.5 crore the previous year. Tata Trusts holds roughly 66% of the holding company.

Air India's Deepening Crisis

The profit numbers, however, exist alongside the group's most expensive problem. Air India lost approximately ₹22,000 crore in FY26 — roughly $2.4 billion — a figure that Bloomberg reported far exceeded the airline's own earlier estimate of $1.6 billion.

Singapore Airlines, which acquired a 25.1% stake when its subsidiary Vistara merged with Air India in 2024, disclosed losses of S$945.2 million (US$742.4 million) from its share of the airline in its full-year earnings. Extrapolating from SIA's stake, analysts at Mint estimated Air India Group's total loss could be as high as ₹28,400 crore.

"Even the newer businesses have performed strongly despite being in their investment and gestation phase. Across the group, existing businesses have been pushed to grow aggressively."

— Executive close to Tata Sons, per The Economic Times

What Went Wrong at Air India

The airline's troubles compounded throughout the year. Pakistan's closure of its airspace to Indian carriers following the India-Pakistan military standoff in May 2025 forced Air India's long-haul flights to the US and Europe onto longer, costlier routes.

In June 2025, a Boeing 787 Dreamliner crash killed more than 240 people, forcing the airline to cut both domestic and international flights. The West Asia conflict made things worse — Air India derives 16% of its capacity from the region, and hostilities shut down much of that market while further rerouting transatlantic flights.

Elevated jet fuel prices and U.S. tariffs on Indian goods, combined with tighter restrictions on foreign worker visas that dampened demand on key routes, completed the damage. CEO Campbell Wilson announced last week that he plans to step down later this year.

The financial crisis has prompted Tata Group and Singapore Airlines to begin discussions on fresh capital infusion, though Bloomberg reported the amounts under consideration may not fully cover what the airline needs.

The Capital Allocation Debate

Air India is not the only cash burner. Tata Sons' unlisted ventures together posted net losses exceeding ₹10,905 crore in FY25, and internal estimates suggest FY26 losses could widen to nearly ₹29,000 crore, with Air India and Tata Digital accounting for the bulk.

At a board review on May 26, directors examined whether the pace of investment across the group's long-gestation businesses needs recalibration. Some raised concerns about capital allocation, particularly as TCS — the group's primary cash generator — moderated its dividend payout to Tata Sons, paying ₹28,292 crore in FY26 compared to ₹32,184 crore the previous year.

Proxy advisory firm InGovern has publicly argued that Tata Sons' structure creates a "closed-loop system of capital consumption," where cash from listed companies funds long-gestation projects at the holding level without direct minority shareholder oversight.

What Comes Next

Tata Sons is expected to publish its full financial results in July. Air India, as a private company, will file its accounts with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs in August.

For the group, the strategic question remains whether it can sustain the heavy investment required across aviation, semiconductors (through Tata Electronics), and digital businesses while keeping returns flowing to shareholders. The answer depends in large part on whether Air India's turnaround plan — now in its fourth year — begins producing operational improvement rather than deepening losses.
nri_angle: Air India's service disruptions and costlier rerouted flights directly affect the Indian diaspora, particularly on high-traffic US, UK, and Gulf routes that connect families across continents.
